lead: The channel coding theorem says noise sets a speed limit, not a wall. For a discrete memoryless channel with capacity C bits per channel use, every code rate R below C has some long code whose decoding error can be made as small as you want. Above C, no code and no decoder can do that. The theorem promises existence, not a construction. It explains why repetition, parity checks and modern long codes help, and it gives the target that practical coding gain is measured against.
prereq: You need: channel capacity and entropy, and the idea of independent bit errors.

sections.h3: Code rate, redundancy and the theorem

blocks.text: Channel coding adds parity bits to message bits before transmission. A block code takes k message bits and sends n coded bits. Its code rate is R = k/n. R is information bits per channel use, not a bit rate in bit/s. The extra fraction 1 − R is the redundancy. For k = 100 and n = 150, R = 0.667 and redundancy is 0.333.

blocks.where: k is the number of message bits per block; n is the number of transmitted bits per block; R is the code rate in information bits per channel use.

blocks.text: The theorem is stated for a discrete memoryless channel (DMC). In a DMC the output at any time depends only on the input at that time and on independent noise; past inputs do not change the present output rule. Let C be the channel capacity from Chapter 7.4, in bits per channel use.
R < C ⇒ Pₑ → 0 as n → ∞;   R > C ⇒ Pₑ ≥ ε > 0
blocks.where: C is the channel capacity in bits per channel use; P<sub>e</sub> is the probability that the decoder output differs from the k message bits; ε is some positive number that depends on the channel and R.

blocks.text: One proof uses random coding. Choose 2<sup>nR</sup> codewords independently from the input distribution that achieves C. For large n, a received word is likely near its own codeword and far from the others, because typical noise sequences form a small set. Nearest-codeword decoding has small average error over the random code. Some code in that set must be at least as good as the average.
For the binary symmetric channel (BSC) with crossover probability p, C = 1 − H(p). At p = 0.01, C = 0.919 bits per channel use. A rate 0.5 is allowed; 0.95 is not.

The theorem promises existence. It does not name a code. It says a code of some length n exists with small P<sub>e</sub>, but not how to build it. It gives no bound on delay, memory or decoder complexity. A code with n = 10,000 may need a large buffer and a complex decoder. It also does not say P<sub>e</sub> is zero at finite n. At finite n, P<sub>e</sub> is small but positive.

Coding gain is the saving in required signal-to-noise ratio at a fixed error rate. Compare an uncoded link and a coded link that reach the same P<sub>e</sub>. Use energy per information bit, E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>. If uncoded needs 10 dB and coded needs 7 dB at the same error rate, the coding gain is 3 dB.

blocks.where: γ<sub>u</sub> and γ<sub>c</sub> are the values of E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>, as power ratios, that the uncoded and the coded link need for the same error rate; E<sub>b</sub> is the energy per information bit in joules and N<sub>0</sub> the one-sided noise power spectral density in W/Hz.

blocks.text: The formula needs linear power ratios, not decibel values. Convert first with E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10<sup>dB/10</sup>. So 10 dB becomes 10 and 7 dB becomes 5.01, and 10 log₁₀(10/5.01) = 3.0 dB. That is simply the difference of the two dB numbers, so with decibel figures you can subtract and get the same answer.

Above capacity the converse holds. If R > C, every decoder has P<sub>e</sub> above a positive floor, no matter how clever. A decoder cannot create information the channel did not deliver. It can only choose the most likely message. A scheme that claims zero error above C is wrong.

The repetition code sends each message bit n times, with n odd. The decoder takes a majority vote. For n = 3, R = 1/3; a decoded bit is wrong only when two or three copies are wrong. For independent bit errors with probability p, P<sub>b</sub> = 3p²(1 − p) + p³. At p = 0.01 this is 2.98 × 10<sup>−4</sup>, much below 0.01. With n = 5 the vote fails only when three or more copies are wrong: P<sub>b</sub> = 9.85 × 10<sup>−6</sup>, but the rate falls to 0.2. Repetition buys a lower error rate only by giving rate away, which is exactly the trade the theorem says a good long code avoids.

Single parity check appends one bit so every codeword has an even number of 1s. With k message bits, n = k + 1 and R = k/(k+1). The receiver checks parity. Any odd number of bit errors makes parity odd and is detected. An even number of errors is not detected. A parity check detects errors but cannot correct them by itself; retransmission or a stronger code is needed.

These elementary codes show the trade. Repetition corrects errors but spends most bits on copies. Parity check spends one bit and detects simple errors cheaply. The theorem says better long codes exist below capacity; Chapter 7.6 to 7.9 build them.

figure.caption: The worked example's 3-fold repetition code on a BSC with p = 0.01: a single flipped copy is outvoted, so the decoded error falls to 2.98 × 10⁻⁴. Its rate 1/3 sits far below the capacity 0.919, which is the room a better long code would use.

examples.question: A binary symmetric channel has crossover probability p = 0.01. Each message bit is sent three times and the receiver takes a majority vote. Find the code rate, the decoded bit error probability, and compare the rate with capacity.
steps: For a 3-repeat code, k = 1 and n = 3. Code rate R = k/n = 1/3 = 0.333.
A decoded bit is wrong when exactly two copies are wrong or when all three are wrong. The two cases cannot happen together, so their probabilities add.
Two wrong copies: choose which 2 of 3 are wrong in 3 ways. Probability = 3p²(1 − p) = 3 × (0.01)² × 0.99 = 0.000297.
Total decoded bit error probability P<sub>b</sub> = 0.000297 + 0.000001 = 0.000298 = 2.98 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Uncoded p = 0.01, so the error falls by a factor of 0.01/0.000298 = 33.6.
Capacity of the BSC: C = 1 − H(p) = 1 − [−p log₂ p − (1 − p) log₂(1 − p)]. With p = 0.01, H(p) = 0.0808 and C = 0.919 bits per channel use.
R = 0.333 < C = 0.919. The theorem allows arbitrarily small error with longer codes; this 3-repeat code is only a short example.
examples.answer: R = 0.333, P<sub>b</sub> = 0.000298, and C = 0.919 bits per channel use, so R < C and the theorem allows the gain.
examples.check:
import math
p = 0.01
R = 1/3
P = 3*p**2*(1-p) + p**3
H = -(p*math.log2(p) + (1-p)*math.log2(1-p))
C = 1 - H
print(round(R, 3))
print(round(P, 6))
print(round(C, 3))

traps: Treating the theorem as a construction. It proves that a code exists; it does not give the parity-check matrix, encoder or decoder.
Believing a better decoder can push P<sub>e</sub> to zero when R > C. The converse forbids it for every decoder.
Calling R = k/n a bit rate in bit/s. R is information bits per channel use; the bit rate also needs the channel symbol rate.
Using p = 1% as p = 1 in H(p). Probabilities in entropy formulas must be between 0 and 1; 1% is 0.01.
Thinking a single parity check corrects one error. It detects an odd number of errors; it does not locate or correct them.

quiz.q: State the channel coding theorem for a DMC in one sentence.
quiz.a: For a DMC with capacity C, every rate R < C has some code with P<sub>e</sub> → 0 as n → ∞; every rate R > C has P<sub>e</sub> bounded away from 0.

quiz.q: Why does the theorem not give an encoder?
quiz.a: It is an existence proof. Random coding shows the average over many random codes is good, so at least one is good, but it does not identify that code or a practical decoder.

quiz.q: A block code has k = 100 message bits and n = 150 coded bits. Find R and redundancy.
A student designs a decoder for R = 1.2C and claims P<sub>e</sub> ≈ 0. Explain the error.
quiz.a: R > C violates the converse. No decoder can make P<sub>e</sub> tend to zero; P<sub>e</sub> has a positive floor. The claim confuses decoder cleverness with the information limit.

quiz.q: What does a single parity check detect?
quiz.a: All odd numbers of bit errors. It does not detect even numbers of errors.

quiz.q: Compare repetition and single parity check for error control.
quiz.a: Repetition with odd n corrects up to (n−1)/2 errors but rate is 1/n. Single parity check has rate k/(k+1), detects odd errors, corrects none. Repetition is stronger per block but costly; parity is cheap detection for retransmission.

quiz.q: Can the (7,4) Hamming code, or any code of rate 4/7, give an arbitrarily small error probability on a BSC with p = 0.1?
quiz.a: C = 1 − H(0.1) = 1 − 0.469 = 0.531 bits per use. The rate is 4/7 = 0.571, which is above C, so by the converse no code of that rate can make P<sub>e</sub> tend to 0. A rate below 0.531, for example 1/2, is needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical systems use LDPC codes in Wi-Fi and 5G data channels, turbo codes in some deep-space links, and polar codes in 5G control channels. Search for the Shannon limit, EXIT charts, density evolution and the channel coding theorem converse. Software-defined radio kits let you measure the gap to capacity with a real decoder.
